lead: Solids differ because their electrons are allowed only in energy bands. The highest filled band is the valence band. The next band is the conduction band. The gap between them is the band gap E<sub>g</sub>. Metals have no gap, insulators have a large gap, semiconductors have a small gap. Doping shifts the Fermi level and adds donor or acceptor levels. This controls conductivity in silicon chips, solar cells, LEDs and UPI card readers. Only a few universities teach this band-structure tutorial.
prereq: You need Unit 1, Chemical Bonding and Coordination Compounds: molecular orbital theory and bonding in solids.

sections.h3: Bands decide metal, insulator or semiconductor

blocks.text: A band is a range of allowed electron energies in a solid. The valence band is the highest band that is normally filled. The conduction band is the next band, normally empty at 0 K. The band gap E<sub>g</sub> is the energy gap between them. A metal has a partly filled conduction band, so electrons move easily. An insulator has a large E<sub>g</sub>, so very few electrons reach the conduction band. A semiconductor has a small E<sub>g</sub>, about 1 eV. At 300 K, some electrons cross it. The Fermi level is the energy where the probability of occupation is 1/2 at equilibrium. In an intrinsic semiconductor it lies near the middle of the gap. Absorption: a photon creates an electron-hole pair only if hν ≥ E<sub>g</sub>.

blocks.where: E is photon energy in eV; h is Planck's constant; c is the speed of light; λ is wavelength in nm. With hc = 1240 eV·nm, E = 1240 ÷ λ.

sections.h3: Doping adds levels and moves the Fermi level

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this 'semiconductor materials'. Doping means adding a small amount of impurity to a pure semiconductor. Pure silicon is intrinsic. Group V donors such as P or As add an electron that sits on a donor level just below the conduction band. The material is n-type: electrons are the majority carriers. Group III acceptors such as B or Al create a hole on an acceptor level just above the valence band. The material is p-type: holes are the majority carriers. Doping raises conductivity but does not close E<sub>g</sub>. The Fermi level moves toward the conduction band for n-type and toward the valence band for p-type. The crystal stays electrically neutral.

items: n-type: donor level near conduction band; electrons are majority carriers.
p-type: acceptor level near valence band; holes are majority carriers.
Direct gap: GaAs; a photon alone excites an electron. Indirect gap: Si and Ge; a phonon is also needed.

figure.caption: Doping adds donor or acceptor levels near the bands, and the Fermi level moves.

spec.aria: A stack shows the conduction band, donor level, Fermi level, acceptor level and valence band from higher to lower energy.

examples.question: Silicon has a band gap E<sub>g</sub> = 1.12 eV at 300 K. Find the longest wavelength of light that silicon can absorb. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm.
steps: A photon is absorbed by a band-to-band transition only if its energy is at least E<sub>g</sub>.
The longest wavelength corresponds to the minimum photon energy, E = E<sub>g</sub> = 1.12 eV.
Use E = hc ÷ λ, so λ = hc ÷ E<sub>g</sub>.
examples.answer: λ = 1107.14 nm ≈ 1107 nm (1.10714 μm), so silicon can absorb light up to about 1107 nm.
examples.check:
hc = 1240
Eg = 1.12
lam = hc / Eg
print(f'{lam:.2f}')
print(round(lam))
print(f'{lam/1000:.5f}')

traps: Doping raises conductivity but does not close the band gap; the gap of silicon stays near 1.12 eV at low doping.
n-type means donor electrons, not a negatively charged crystal; the crystal remains neutral.
Do not swap the levels: donor levels sit near the conduction band, acceptor levels near the valence band.
The longest absorbed wavelength uses the minimum energy E<sub>g</sub>: λ = hc ÷ E<sub>g</sub>, not E<sub>g</sub> ÷ hc.
Direct and indirect gaps differ in momentum; GaAs is direct, Si and Ge are indirect, so their absorption strengths differ.

quiz.q: Define valence band and conduction band.
quiz.a: Valence band: the highest band that is normally filled. Conduction band: the next band, normally empty at 0 K.

quiz.q: Why does an n-type crystal remain electrically neutral after adding donor atoms?
quiz.a: Each donor atom contributes one free electron but also a positive ion core; the extra electron balances the core charge, so the whole crystal has no net charge.

quiz.q: Ge has E<sub>g</sub> = 0.66 eV. Find the longest wavelength it can absorb. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm.
Compare n-type and p-type doping: dopant group, majority carrier, and Fermi-level shift.
quiz.a: n-type: group V donor, electrons majority, Fermi level moves toward conduction band. p-type: group III acceptor, holes majority, Fermi level moves toward valence band.

quiz.q: Why is GaAs called a direct-band-gap material while Si is indirect?
quiz.a: In GaAs the conduction-band minimum and valence-band maximum have the same momentum, so a photon alone can excite an electron. In Si they have different momentum, so a phonon is also needed.

quiz.q: A photon of energy 1.00 eV strikes silicon with E<sub>g</sub> = 1.12 eV. Is it absorbed by a band-to-band transition? Explain.
quiz.a: No. 1.00 eV < 1.12 eV, so the photon energy is below the band gap and cannot create an electron-hole pair across the gap.

quiz.q: Explain why a metal has high conductivity using bands, and why an insulator does not.
quiz.a: Metal: a partly filled band has empty states next to filled states, so electrons move under a small field. Insulator: a full valence band is separated from an empty conduction band by a large E<sub>g</sub>, so few carriers exist.
The energy at which the occupation probability is 1/2 at equilibrium.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real chips use doping profiles, carrier mobility and contact metals, not just a single donor level. Solar cells and photodiodes use the absorption edge; LEDs need a direct gap for efficient light emission. Search next: Hall effect, carrier concentration, p-n junction band diagram, and thin-film deposition (see 6.7).
